Data: [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/), Palmer Station Antarctica LTER, released under the [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) licence. Cite as Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). I use the copy that ships inside the `palmerpenguins` Python package, so nothing is downloaded when the site is built.

The dataset has measurements for 344 penguins from three species: Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo. In this post I do the same kind of analysis as in my R post, but in Python with pandas and matplotlib. I ask how body mass differs between species, how it relates to flipper length, and how it differs between males and females.

## Loading the data

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| warning: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt 
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
```

```{python}
#| label: load-data
penguins = load_penguins()
print("Rows in the raw data:", penguins.shape[0])

penguins_data = penguins.dropna(
    subset=["species", "sex", "body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm"]
)
print("Rows after dropping missing values:", penguins_data.shape[0])

penguins_data.head()
```

I removed rows with missing values in the variables used in this analysis.

## Comparing body mass by species

```{python}
#| label: species-summary
average_mass = (
    penguins_data.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"]
    .agg(mean_body_mass_g="mean", median_body_mass_g="median", n="count")
    .round(1)
)
average_mass
```

Body mass differs between the three species. Gentoo penguins have the highest average body mass, while Adelie penguins have the lowest.

## Body mass and flipper length

```{python}
#| label: fig-penguin-mass-py
#| fig-cap: "Body mass and flipper length of Palmer Penguins by species."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
for species, group in penguins_data.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(
        group["flipper_length_mm"],
        group["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.7,
    )
ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: correlation
corr = penguins_data["flipper_length_mm"].corr(penguins_data["body_mass_g"])
print(f"Correlation between flipper length and body mass: {corr:.2f}")
```

The figure shows a strong positive relationship: penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier. The correlation is about `{python} f"{corr:.2f}"`. The species also form fairly distinct groups, with Gentoo penguins in the top right.

## Comparing males and females

```{python}
#| label: sex-summary
sex_mass = (
    penguins_data.groupby(["species", "sex"], as_index=False)["body_mass_g"]
    .mean()
    .rename(columns={"body_mass_g": "mean_body_mass_g"})
    .round(1)
)
sex_mass
```

In every species the males are heavier than the females on average.

## Conclusion

Using the Palmer Penguins data in Python, I found clear differences in body mass between species, a strong positive link between flipper length and body mass, and a consistent difference between the sexes. These simple summaries show how pandas and matplotlib can be used to explore a real dataset.
